title: Caste and Its Challengers
objective: After this level you can explain how caste shaped South Asian society and how Buddhists, Sikhs, devotional poets and B. R. Ambedkar challenged it.
summary: Caste ranked people by birth. The Buddha, Ravidas, the Sikh langar, Hindu reformers and B. R. Ambedkar challenged it, and India's 1950 constitution abolished untouchability.

cards.headline: Can a society rank people by birth, and can faith push back?
cards.body: For centuries, caste shaped whom people in South Asia married and what work they did. Here is how it worked, and the religious voices, inside Hinduism and beyond it, that pushed back.

cards.headline: Varna and jati
cards.body: Ancient texts describe four varnas: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, an arrangement traced to a hymn in the Rigveda. Daily life ran on a finer grid of jatis, birth groups that traditionally married within themselves and were tied to hereditary occupations. People assigned work seen as impure, such as handling dead animals, were treated as untouchable. Many in these communities now prefer the name Dalit.

cards.headline: Not by birth
cards.body: Challenges are old. In a Buddhist discourse, the Buddha teaches that no one is an outcast or a brahman by birth; by deeds one becomes either. The bhakti poet Ravidas, born into a leatherworking caste considered untouchable, sang that all are made from the same clay by the same creator. About 40 of his poems stand in the Sikh scripture.

cards.headline: At the table and in reform
cards.body: Sikhs made the point at mealtime: the langar, Britannica notes, began as a protest against the caste system. Within Hinduism, reformers argued too. The Arya Samaj, founded by Dayananda Sarasvati in 1875, opposed basing caste on birth rather than merit and rejected untouchability entirely.

cards.headline: Ambedkar: a constitution and a new path
cards.body: B. R. Ambedkar, born into a Dalit Mahar family, chaired the committee that drafted India's constitution. It came into force on 26 January 1950: Article 15 bans discrimination based on caste, and Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Ambedkar despaired that untouchability persisted in Hindu doctrine, and in October 1956 he became a Buddhist at a ceremony in Nagpur, joined by a vast crowd of fellow Dalits.

cards.headline: Caste and Its Challengers: the takeaways
learned: Caste ranked people by birth into varnas and jatis
The Buddha, Ravidas, the langar and the Arya Samaj challenged it

questions.prompt: Match each name from the story of caste and its challengers with what this level says about it.
questions.explanation: Article 15 bans discrimination based on caste and Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Dayananda Sarasvati founded the Arya Samaj, and Ravidas was a bhakti poet.

questions.prompt: The Buddha and the Arya Samaj lived more than two thousand years apart. What did their challenges to caste share?

options.label: Both said a person's worth depends on birth
Both called for a new state religion
options.rationale: Neither argument was about the state.

options.label: Both judged people by conduct or merit, not birth
Both rejected all scripture
options.rationale: The Arya Samaj upheld the Vedas.

questions.explanation: The Buddha taught that deeds make the brahman; the Arya Samaj opposed caste by birth rather than merit.

questions.prompt: Ravidas and the Arya Samaj rejected caste by birth from within the Hindu world, while others defended it. Which Level 4 idea does this show?

options.label: Myths are false stories
options.rationale: Level 4 said the opposite about myth.

options.label: Every tradition is a family of subtraditions
Scholars rank faiths from best to worst

questions.explanation: No faith speaks with one voice: every tradition is a loosely held-together family of subtraditions.
